results.summary: This design implements an 8-bit shift register with output latches, functionally equivalent to the 74HC595. It accepts serial data and control signals (sclrn, ser, rck, srck, G) and provides 8 parallel outputs. External hardware required includes 8 LEDs or a PMOD LED module. The design has been silicon-tested by the author using a bit-banging program to create a Knight Rider effect.

This design implements the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for evaluating the randomness of a bit source. It accepts one input bit per clock cycle and outputs a valid signal and an is_random flag every 65536 cycles. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for being an HLS implementation of a standard statistical test for random number generators.

This design plays the Super Mario tune on a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It requires a 3125 Hz clock and a brief reset pulse to start playback. External hardware needed is a piezo speaker connected across the two output pins. The design was generated by converting an RTTL ringtone into Verilog using Python.

This design converts an 8-bit binary input into signals to drive a 7-segment display showing hexadecimal digits. It accepts 8 input bits and outputs 8 bits for the 7-segment display segments. External hardware required is a 7-segment display. The documentation is minimal, with placeholder text for how it works and how to test.

This design implements a RISC-V CPU called LaRVa with a serial port, JTAG interface, and a few peripherals. It requires external SRAM memory and address latches attached to PMOD connectors for full operation. The bootloader allows programs to be loaded via serial at 115200 bps. The design is notable for including a JTAG debug interface and being a complete CPU project.

This design implements a 4-bit successive approximation analog-to-digital converter. It requires an external sample-and-hold circuit to hold the analog input constant during conversion. The conversion takes 5 clock cycles at 5 MHz, yielding a 1 MHz conversion rate. The digital output is available on four output pins after an end-of-conversion signal.

This design implements a simple one-stage RISC-V CPU based on a university lecture. Instructions are 32-bit but loaded over four clock cycles via an 8-bit input bus. The CPU outputs the ALU result on 8 output pins. The design is not yet shipped and is intended for educational purposes.

This design is a factory test module that either mirrors inputs to outputs or outputs a counter depending on a select input. When input 0 is high, a counter is output on all outputs and bidirectional pins; otherwise inputs are mirrored. No external hardware is required. The design is simple and intended for testing the chip.

This design implements an 8-bit Concurrent Built-In Logic Block Observer (CBILBO) shift register for memory testing. It uses logic gates, D flip-flops, and multiplexers for shifting and feedback operations. No external hardware is required. The design is intended for built-in self-test applications.

This design displays a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display based on a 6-bit DIP switch input. It requires a high clock rate (e.g., 1 kHz) to drive the segments sequentially. External hardware needed is a 7-segment display. The design has been silicon-tested and works as intended.
